before.title: Confessions
before.author: Augustine of Hippo
before.openingText: Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee. Grant me, Lord, to know and understand which is first, to call on Thee or to praise Thee?
before.about:
The Confessions is the spiritual autobiography of Augustine of Hippo, written in his forties as he was settling into the bishop's chair of a small North African town. It tells the story of his life from infancy through his conversion to Christianity at thirty-one and the death of his mother shortly after. The narrative moves through his theft of pears as a teenager, his early ambition as a rhetorician in Carthage, the long affair that produced his son Adeodatus, his nine years inside the Manichean sect, his disillusion with Roman astrology, his discovery of Plotinus, his collapse in a Milanese garden under the words of a child singing tolle, lege — "take up and read" — and his baptism by Ambrose at Easter 387. The last three books leave autobiography behind for sustained meditation on memory, time, and the opening of Genesis.

Augustine wrote it in Latin around 397–400 CE, addressing the entire book to God as a prolonged prayer rather than to a human reader. He had recently been made bishop of Hippo Regius, a port town in what is now Algeria, and the Confessions was in part an answer to people who suspected his Manichean past. Thirteen books, roughly 100,000 words, structured so that the first nine narrate his life, the tenth examines his present soul, and the final three turn outward to scripture and creation.

It is the founding work of Western autobiography and one of the most influential books in Christian thought. Augustine invented a genre — the prolonged inward look at one's own soul, narrated as a confession before God — that did not exist in classical literature. Petrarch carried a copy up Mont Ventoux and opened it at random. Rousseau took the title for his own Confessions thirteen centuries later and reversed its theology. Wittgenstein read it constantly in the last years of his life. Almost every memoir written in the West that takes its own subjectivity seriously is downstream of what Augustine did in this book.

angleCards.title: The invention of the inner self.
angleCards.text: Augustine is the first Western writer to treat the inner life as the primary subject. Before him, literature looked outward — at deeds, gods, fate. I want to read the Confessions as the founding document of psychological introspection, noticing each time he turns inward.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Confessions as the origin of the inner self — the text where Augustine invented the kind of introspection we now take entirely for granted.

angleCards.title: The theology of restlessness.
angleCards.text: Augustine's most famous sentence is a diagnosis, not just a prayer. I want to test his claim — that there is a specific quality of longing in human life that cannot be satisfied by any finite object — against my own experience and everything else I have read.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the theology of restlessness — "our heart is restless until it rests in Thee" — and decide whether it is true as a description of human experience, regardless of whether one believes in God.

angleCards.title: Philosophy inside autobiography.
angleCards.text: Books X–XIII leave the narrative behind and become something stranger — extended meditations on memory, time, and the meaning of Genesis 1. I want to read those final books as philosophy and understand why Augustine embedded them in a personal confession rather than a separate treatise.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Books X through XIII as philosophical treatises embedded in an autobiography — Augustine's extended meditations on memory, time, and the nature of creation.

angleCards.title: The figure of Monica.
angleCards.text: Augustine's mother prays for him for decades and never stops believing he will convert. Her faith is tested for years and vindicated. I want to read the Monica sections carefully — understanding what she represents theologically and why her death in Book IX is the emotional centre of the whole work.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand Augustine's relationship to his mother Monica — what she represents in the architecture of the book, and why her death is placed where it is.

cast.name: Augustine
cast.description: Writing in his forties as bishop of Hippo, looking back on a man he no longer is. The young Augustine of the narrative is brilliant, sexually restless, ambitious for the rhetorical career that took him to Rome and then Milan, and sincerely trying every philosophical system that crosses his path before giving in to the one he had been resisting. He addresses God on every page as the only adequate reader of his own life.

cast.name: Monica
cast.description: A devout North African Christian who prays for her son's conversion for thirty years and refuses to stop believing it will happen. She follows him from Thagaste to Carthage to Rome to Milan when he tries to leave her behind. After his baptism, she tells him at the port of Ostia that her work is finished, and she dies a few days later. The Ostia vision and her death in Book IX are the emotional climax of the autobiographical half of the book.

cast.name: Ambrose
cast.description: The man who finally makes Christianity intellectually credible to Augustine, not by argument but by example. Augustine, attending Ambrose's sermons at first only to study his rhetoric, finds the content getting in. He also notices Ambrose reading silently to himself — an unusual practice in the ancient world — and begins to suspect a kind of inner attention he has not found in the Manichees. Ambrose baptizes Augustine at the Easter vigil of 387.

cast.name: Alypius
cast.description: A younger man from Augustine's hometown who follows him to Carthage, to Rome, and to Milan, sharing every stage of his intellectual restlessness. The book records Alypius getting hooked on the gladiatorial games against his own resolve — "he opened his eyes and was wounded in his soul" — as a parable of how the will fails. Alypius is in the garden at Milan when Augustine reads Romans 13 and breaks; he reads the next verse and converts in the same hour.

cast.name: The Unnamed Boy
cast.description: A child Augustine hears chanting tolle, lege — "take up and read" — in a neighbor's garden in Milan in 386. Augustine takes it as a divine instruction, opens the letter of Paul lying on the bench, and reads Romans 13:13–14. The child is never identified, never seen, possibly imagined. The scene became the founding image in Christian literature of conversion arriving from outside, through ordinary speech, at the moment the soul is finally ready to hear it.

cast.name: God
cast.description: Not a character in the narrative but the only audience Augustine writes for. Every sentence of the Confessions is addressed in the second person to God, who is treated as already knowing everything in the book and as the one in whose presence the speaking happens. This formal choice changes the whole genre. The reader is overhearing a prayer, not being told a story. Most of what makes the book strange and intimate flows from this single decision.

whyItMatters.title: The Founding of Inwardness
whyItMatters.body: Before Augustine, Western literature had little of what is now called psychological depth. Homer's heroes are great but largely consistent. Greek tragedy works through deeds and choruses. Roman autobiography, in Caesar or Marcus Aurelius, looks outward at campaigns or maxims. The Confessions is the first sustained attempt in Western prose to describe what it is like from the inside to be a divided self — the wanting that contradicts itself, the will that cannot make itself want what it knows it should want, the memory that hides things from its owner. Augustine watches himself and asks how the watching is possible. Rousseau, Pascal, Bunyan, Newman, Merton, and almost every modern memoirist who takes interior life seriously is working in territory Augustine opened. Modern AI debates about machine consciousness are still arguing in his categories.

whyItMatters.title: Conversion as a Real Event
whyItMatters.body: Book VIII contains the scene that would become the master template of Christian conversion narrative: Augustine in a Milan garden, weeping under a fig tree, hearing a child's voice say tolle, lege, picking up the letter of Paul, reading one sentence, and rising up changed. He had been intellectually persuaded for years and could not move his will. The book records the gap between believing and being able to act on what you believe — a gap that any honest reader recognizes whether or not they share the theology. The structure of the scene shows up later in John Wesley at Aldersgate, in C.S. Lewis on the bus to Whipsnade, in countless smaller stories. Augustine made the form. He also showed it from inside, with the doubt and self-suspicion intact.

whyItMatters.title: The Question of Time
whyItMatters.body: Book XI turns from autobiography to one of the most concentrated passages of philosophy in any language: an examination of what time is. Augustine asks how the past can exist if it is gone, how the future can exist if it has not arrived, how the present can have any duration if any duration can be divided into past and future. He arrives at a model in which time exists as the soul's distentio — its stretching across memory, attention, and expectation. The argument has stayed alive for sixteen centuries because the questions have not closed. Wittgenstein read this section repeatedly. Husserl built phenomenology partly around it. Recent work in cognitive science on the experience of duration still cites Book XI.

after.title: Confessions
after.author: Augustine of Hippo
after.openingText: You made us for Yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in You.
after.about:
Augustine tells the story of his life as a prayer to God. Childhood, education, ambition, friendship, sexual desire, grief, and religious searching become occasions to ask why people want things that do not satisfy them and why knowing the good does not guarantee doing it. The narrative moves from North Africa to Rome and Milan, where Augustine hears Ambrose preach, encounters books of the Platonists, and undergoes the garden experience described in Book VIII. Book IX recounts his baptism and his mother Monica’s death.

The thirteen books have a deliberate change of direction. Books I–IX look back over his life. Book X examines his present condition, including memory, desire, and the temptations that remain after conversion. Book XI asks what time is. Books XII–XIII interpret the opening of Genesis, exploring creation, different possible readings of scripture, and the hope of rest in God. The closing books are part of the work’s argument, not an appendix to the life story.

Confessions combines autobiography, philosophy, biblical interpretation, and worship. The word “confession” includes admitting wrongdoing, acknowledging faith, and praising God. Readers need not share Augustine’s beliefs to follow his close examination of habit, divided intention, memory, and self-deception. His account also belongs to late antiquity: it includes assumptions about gender, authority, and religion that should be read as his claims rather than as present-day guidance.

angleCards.title: A divided will
angleCards.text: Augustine can recognize a better course without being able to choose it wholeheartedly. Follow the gap between conviction, habit, and action, especially in Book VIII.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand Augustine’s account of a divided will and how habits shape action.

angleCards.title: Restlessness and desire
angleCards.text: The opening prayer connects human restlessness with the search for God. Ask what Augustine thinks people are seeking in pleasure, praise, knowledge, and friendship.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine Augustine’s claim that lasting rest requires a change in what we love.

angleCards.title: Memory, time, and creation
angleCards.text: Read Book X on memory, Book XI on time, and Books XII–XIII on Genesis. Notice how the philosophical questions grow out of the prayer rather than leaving it behind.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the arguments about memory, time, and creation in Books X–XIII.

angleCards.title: Monica and the telling of a life
angleCards.text: Read Monica’s dreams, prayers, advice, shared conversation at Ostia, and death alongside Augustine’s portrayal of his own development. Distinguish her reported words from the meaning he later gives them.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand Monica’s role and how Augustine shapes his account of their relationship.

cast.name: Augustine
cast.description: The older narrator addresses God while examining his younger self. He recounts his career as a teacher of rhetoric, his involvement with the Manichaeans, and his movement toward Christian faith. His recollections also question how well he knows his own motives.

cast.name: Monica
cast.description: A Christian whose prayers and concern run through the narrative. Book IX describes her life, her conversation with Augustine at Ostia, and her death. Augustine presents her conduct through the religious and social expectations of his time.

cast.name: Ambrose
cast.description: Augustine first listens to his preaching for its eloquence and gradually finds that its interpretations answer objections he had raised against scripture. Ambrose baptizes Augustine in Book IX. Augustine also describes his habit of silent reading.

cast.name: Alypius
cast.description: A friend from Augustine’s hometown who shares his intellectual and religious journey. His attraction to gladiatorial spectacles illustrates the force of habit. He is present during the conversion scene in Book VIII and is later baptized with Augustine.

cast.name: The unidentified child
cast.description: Augustine hears a child chanting “Take up and read” from a neighboring house. He explicitly says he does not know whether it is a boy or a girl. He interprets the words as a divine instruction and reads a passage from Paul.

cast.name: God
cast.description: Augustine addresses God as the one who already knows his life. He also discusses his human readers and sometimes addresses them directly. Readers thus encounter both a prayer and an account written to be shared.

whyItMatters.title: Self-examination in narrative
whyItMatters.body: The work makes ordinary recollections carry difficult questions: why steal something one does not need, why enjoy grief in a theatre, why seek praise, and why struggle to act on a settled conviction? Augustine’s explanations can be questioned, but the movement between an episode and the scrutiny of its motives gives the book much of its force.

whyItMatters.title: Conversion and continuing difficulty
whyItMatters.body: The garden scene in Book VIII does not end the examination of the self. Book X returns to temptations involving desire, food, music, curiosity, and praise. Reading these sections together prevents conversion from becoming merely a neat ending to the story.

whyItMatters.title: An argument about time
whyItMatters.body: Book XI asks how past, present, and future can be understood when the past is gone, the future has not arrived, and the present has no duration. Examples involving speech, syllables, and a familiar song lead Augustine toward memory, attention, and expectation. Follow the steps of the argument rather than treating its best-known question as a stand-alone quotation.

reason: Replace retained guide with source-grounded introduction; correct child’s unknown sex, book structure, God/human readership, Ambrose’s interpretive role; remove unsupported first-ever and reception claims; fully modernize Danish.

before.title: Confessions
before.author: Augustine of Hippo
before.openingText: Du vækker os, så vi finder glæde i at prise Dig, for Du har skabt os til Dig selv, og vort hjerte er uroligt, indtil det hviler i Dig. Forund mig, Herre, at vide og forstå, hvad der kommer først — at påkalde Dig eller at prise Dig?
before.about:
Bekendelser er den åndelige selvbiografi af Augustin af Hippo, skrevet i hans fyrrere, mens han faldt til rette i bispestolen i en lille nordafrikansk by. Den fortæller historien om hans liv fra barndommen frem til hans omvendelse til kristendommen som enogtredveårig og hans mors død kort efter. Fortællingen bevæger sig gennem hans tyveri af pærer som teenager, hans tidlige ambitioner som retoriker i Kartago, det lange forhold, der gav ham sønnen Adeodatus, hans ni år inden i den manikæiske sekt, hans skuffelse over romersk astrologi, hans opdagelse af Plotin, hans sammenbrud i en have i Milano under et barns sang tolle, lege — »tag og læs« — og hans dåb ved Ambrosius i påsken 387. De sidste tre bøger forlader selvbiografien til fordel for vedholdende meditation over hukommelse, tid og åbningen af Første Mosebog.

Augustin skrev den på latin omkring 397–400 e.Kr. og rettede hele bogen til Gud som en langstrakt bøn snarere end til en menneskelig læser. Han var for nylig blevet biskop af Hippo Regius, en havneby i det nuværende Algeriet, og Bekendelser var til dels et svar til folk, der nærede mistanke til hans manikæiske fortid. Tretten bøger, omtrent 100.000 ord, struktureret så de første ni fortæller hans liv, den tiende undersøger hans nuværende sjæl, og de sidste tre vender udad mod skriften og skabelsen.

Det er den vestlige selvbiografis grundlæggende værk og en af de mest indflydelsesrige bøger i kristen tænkning. Augustin opfandt en genre — det vedholdende indadvendte blik på ens egen sjæl, fortalt som en bekendelse for Gud — som ikke fandtes i klassisk litteratur. Petrarca bar et eksemplar op på Mont Ventoux og slog det op tilfældigt. Rousseau tog titlen til sine egne Bekendelser tretten århundreder senere og vendte dens teologi om. Wittgenstein læste den uafladeligt i de sidste år af sit liv. Næsten enhver erindringsbog skrevet i Vesten, der tager sin egen subjektivitet alvorligt, er afledt af det, Augustin gjorde i denne bog.

angleCards.title: Det indre selvs opfindelse.
angleCards.text: Augustin er den første vestlige forfatter, der behandler det indre liv som det primære emne. Før ham vendte litteraturen blikket udad — mod gerninger, guder, skæbne. Jeg vil læse Bekendelser som det psykologiske selvransagelses grunddokument og lægge mærke til, hver gang han vender blikket indad.
angleCards.angleObjective: Jeg vil læse Bekendelser som det indre selvs oprindelse — den tekst, hvor Augustin opfandt den slags selvransagelse, vi nu tager fuldstændig for givet.

angleCards.title: Rastløshedens teologi.
angleCards.text: Augustins mest berømte sætning er en diagnose, ikke blot en bøn. Jeg vil afprøve hans påstand — at der findes en bestemt kvalitet af længsel i menneskelivet, som ikke kan tilfredsstilles af noget endeligt objekt — mod min egen erfaring og alt andet, jeg har læst.
angleCards.angleObjective: Jeg vil læse rastløshedens teologi — »vort hjerte er uroligt, indtil det hviler i Dig« — og afgøre, om den er sand som en beskrivelse af menneskelig erfaring, uanset om man tror på Gud.

angleCards.title: Filosofi inden i selvbiografi.
angleCards.text: Bog X–XIII forlader fortællingen og bliver til noget mærkeligere — udstrakte meditationer over hukommelse, tid og betydningen af Første Mosebog 1. Jeg vil læse de sidste bøger som filosofi og forstå, hvorfor Augustin indlejrede dem i en personlig bekendelse snarere end i en separat afhandling.
angleCards.angleObjective: Jeg vil læse Bog X til XIII som filosofiske afhandlinger indlejret i en selvbiografi — Augustins udstrakte meditationer over hukommelse, tid og skabelsens natur.

angleCards.title: Skikkelsen Monica.
angleCards.text: Augustins mor beder for ham i årtier og holder aldrig op med at tro, at han vil omvende sig. Hendes tro prøves i årevis og bekræftes. Jeg vil læse Monica-afsnittene omhyggeligt — forstå, hvad hun repræsenterer teologisk, og hvorfor hendes død i Bog IX er hele værkets følelsesmæssige centrum.
angleCards.angleObjective: Jeg vil forstå Augustins forhold til sin mor Monica — hvad hun repræsenterer i bogens arkitektur, og hvorfor hendes død er placeret, hvor den er.

cast.name: Augustine
cast.description: Skriver i sine fyrrere som biskop af Hippo og ser tilbage på en mand, han ikke længere er. Fortællingens unge Augustin er glimrende, seksuelt rastløs, ambitiøs efter den retoriske karriere, der førte ham til Rom og siden Milano, og forsøger oprigtigt ethvert filosofisk system, der krydser hans vej, før han giver efter for det ene, han havde stået imod. Han henvender sig til Gud på hver side som den eneste tilstrækkelige læser af sit eget liv.

cast.name: Monica
cast.description: En from nordafrikansk kristen, der beder for sin søns omvendelse i tredive år og nægter at holde op med at tro, at den vil ske. Hun følger ham fra Thagaste til Kartago til Rom til Milano, når han forsøger at lade hende blive tilbage. Efter hans dåb fortæller hun ham ved havnen i Ostia, at hendes arbejde er fuldført, og hun dør få dage senere. Synet i Ostia og hendes død i Bog IX er det følelsesmæssige højdepunkt i bogens selvbiografiske halvdel.

cast.name: Ambrose
cast.description: Den mand, der til sidst gør kristendommen intellektuelt troværdig for Augustin, ikke ved argument men ved eksempel. Augustin, der først kun overværer Ambrosius' prædikener for at studere hans retorik, mærker indholdet trænge ind. Han bemærker også, at Ambrosius læser stille for sig selv — en usædvanlig praksis i den antikke verden — og begynder at ane en slags indre opmærksomhed, som han ikke har fundet hos manikæerne. Ambrosius døber Augustin ved påskevigilien i 387.

cast.name: Alypius
cast.description: En yngre mand fra Augustins hjemby, der følger ham til Kartago, til Rom og til Milano og deler hvert trin af hans intellektuelle rastløshed. Bogen beretter, hvordan Alypius bliver hængende ved gladiatorkampene mod sin egen vilje — »han åbnede sine øjne og blev såret i sin sjæl« — som en lignelse om, hvordan viljen svigter. Alypius er i haven i Milano, da Augustin læser Romerbrevet 13 og brister; han læser det næste vers og omvender sig i samme time.

cast.name: The Unnamed Boy
cast.description: Et barn, Augustin hører synge tolle, lege — »tag og læs« — i en nabos have i Milano i 386. Augustin opfatter det som en guddommelig anvisning, åbner Paulus' brev, der ligger på bænken, og læser Romerbrevet 13,13–14. Barnet identificeres aldrig, ses aldrig, er muligvis indbildt. Scenen blev det grundlæggende billede i kristen litteratur på omvendelse, der ankommer udefra, gennem almindelig tale, i det øjeblik sjælen endelig er parat til at høre den.

cast.name: God
cast.description: Ikke en karakter i fortællingen, men det eneste publikum, Augustin skriver for. Hver sætning i Bekendelser er rettet i anden person til Gud, der behandles som en, der allerede ved alt i bogen, og som den, i hvis nærvær talen finder sted. Dette formelle valg ændrer hele genren. Læseren overhører en bøn, bliver ikke fortalt en historie. Det meste af det, der gør bogen mærkelig og intim, udspringer af denne ene beslutning.

whyItMatters.title: Indadvendthedens grundlæggelse
whyItMatters.body: Før Augustin havde vestlig litteratur kun lidt af det, der nu kaldes psykologisk dybde. Homers helte er store, men i vid udstrækning konsistente. Græsk tragedie virker gennem gerninger og korsange. Romersk selvbiografi, hos Cæsar eller Marcus Aurelius, vender blikket udad mod felttog eller leveregler. Bekendelser er det første vedholdende forsøg i vestlig prosa på at beskrive, hvordan det indefra er at være et splittet selv — viljen, der modsiger sig selv, viljen, der ikke kan få sig selv til at ville det, den ved, den burde ville, hukommelsen, der skjuler ting for sin ejer. Augustin betragter sig selv og spørger, hvordan betragtningen er mulig. Rousseau, Pascal, Bunyan, Newman, Merton og næsten enhver moderne erindringsskriver, der tager det indre liv alvorligt, arbejder i et terræn, Augustin åbnede. Moderne AI-debatter om maskinbevidsthed strides stadig i hans kategorier.

whyItMatters.title: Omvendelse som en virkelig begivenhed
whyItMatters.body: Bog VIII indeholder den scene, der skulle blive mesterskabelonen for den kristne omvendelsesfortælling: Augustin i en have i Milano, grædende under et figentræ, der hører et barns stemme sige tolle, lege, samler Paulus' brev op, læser én sætning og rejser sig forandret. Han havde været intellektuelt overbevist i årevis og kunne ikke flytte sin vilje. Bogen beretter om kløften mellem at tro og at kunne handle på det, man tror — en kløft, enhver ærlig læser genkender, uanset om de deler teologien. Scenens struktur dukker op senere hos John Wesley ved Aldersgate, hos C.S. Lewis i bussen til Whipsnade, i utallige mindre historier. Augustin skabte formen. Han viste den også indefra, med tvivlen og selvmistanken intakt.

whyItMatters.title: Spørgsmålet om tid
whyItMatters.body: Bog XI vender sig fra selvbiografi til en af de mest koncentrerede filosofiske passager på noget sprog: en undersøgelse af, hvad tid er. Augustin spørger, hvordan fortiden kan eksistere, hvis den er forbi, hvordan fremtiden kan eksistere, hvis den ikke er ankommet, hvordan nutiden kan have nogen varighed, hvis enhver varighed kan deles i fortid og fremtid. Han når frem til en model, hvor tid eksisterer som sjælens distentio — dens udstrækning over hukommelse, opmærksomhed og forventning. Argumentet har holdt sig i live i seksten århundreder, fordi spørgsmålene ikke er lukket. Wittgenstein læste dette afsnit gentagne gange. Husserl byggede fænomenologien delvis op om det. Nyere arbejde i kognitionsvidenskab om oplevelsen af varighed citerer stadig Bog XI.

after.title: Bekendelser
after.author: Augustin af Hippo
after.openingText: For du har skabt os til dig, og vores hjerte er uroligt, indtil det finder hvile i dig.
after.about:
Augustin fortæller sit liv som en bøn til Gud. Barndom, uddannelse, ambitioner, venskab, seksuelt begær, sorg og religiøs søgen bliver anledninger til at spørge, hvorfor mennesker ønsker noget, som ikke tilfredsstiller dem, og hvorfor erkendelsen af det gode ikke sikrer, at de gør det. Fortællingen går fra Nordafrika til Rom og Milano. Dér hører Augustin Ambrosius prædike, møder platonikernes bøger og oplever den omvendelse i en have, som beskrives i bog VIII. Bog IX fortæller om hans dåb og hans mor Monikas død.

De tretten bøger skifter bevidst retning undervejs. Bog I–IX ser tilbage på hans liv. Bog X undersøger hans nuværende tilstand, blandt andet hukommelsen, begæret og de fristelser, der bliver tilbage efter omvendelsen. Bog XI spørger, hvad tid er. Bog XII–XIII fortolker begyndelsen af Første Mosebog og undersøger skabelsen, forskellige mulige læsninger af Skriften og håbet om hvile i Gud. De afsluttende bøger er en del af værkets argument, ikke et tillæg til livshistorien.

Bekendelser forener selvbiografi, filosofi, bibelfortolkning og lovprisning. Ordet bekendelse omfatter både at indrømme skyld, bekende sin tro og prise Gud. Man behøver ikke dele Augustins tro for at følge hans undersøgelse af vaner, splittet vilje, hukommelse og selvbedrag. Samtidig hører hans beretning hjemme i senantikken. Dens forestillinger om køn, autoritet og religion skal læses som hans synspunkter, ikke som nutidige råd.

angleCards.title: En splittet vilje
angleCards.text: Augustin kan se en bedre vej uden helhjertet at kunne vælge den. Følg afstanden mellem overbevisning, vane og handling, især i bog VIII.
angleCards.angleObjective: Jeg vil forstå Augustins beskrivelse af den splittede vilje og vanernes betydning for vores handlinger.

angleCards.title: Uro og længsel
angleCards.text: Den indledende bøn forbinder menneskets uro med søgen efter Gud. Undersøg, hvad Augustin mener, vi søger i nydelse, ros, viden og venskab.
angleCards.angleObjective: Jeg vil undersøge Augustins påstand om, at varig hvile kræver en forandring af det, vi elsker.

angleCards.title: Hukommelse, tid og skabelse
angleCards.text: Læs bog X om hukommelsen, bog XI om tiden og bog XII–XIII om Første Mosebog. Læg mærke til, hvordan de filosofiske spørgsmål vokser ud af bønnen.
angleCards.angleObjective: Jeg vil følge argumenterne om hukommelse, tid og skabelse i bog X–XIII.

angleCards.title: Monika og fortællingen om et liv
angleCards.text: Læs Monikas drømme, bønner, råd, samtalen i Ostia og hendes død sammen med Augustins beskrivelse af sin egen udvikling. Skeln mellem hendes gengivne ord og den betydning, han senere giver dem.
angleCards.angleObjective: Jeg vil forstå Monikas rolle, og hvordan Augustin former beretningen om deres forhold.

cast.name: Augustin
cast.description: Den ældre fortæller henvender sig til Gud, mens han undersøger sit yngre jeg. Han fortæller om sin karriere som lærer i retorik, sin tilknytning til manikæerne og sin vej mod kristendommen. Undervejs spørger han også, hvor godt han kender sine egne motiver.

cast.name: Monika
cast.description: En kristen, hvis bønner og omsorg løber gennem fortællingen. Bog IX beskriver hendes liv, hendes samtale med Augustin i Ostia og hendes død. Augustin fremstiller hendes handlinger ud fra sin tids religiøse og sociale forventninger.

cast.name: Ambrosius
cast.description: Augustin lytter først til hans prædikener for veltalenhedens skyld. Efterhånden opdager han, at fortolkningerne besvarer nogle af hans indvendinger mod Skriften. Ambrosius døber Augustin i bog IX. Augustin beskriver også hans vane med at læse uden at sige ordene højt.

cast.name: Alypius
cast.description: En ven fra Augustins hjemby, som deler hans intellektuelle og religiøse søgen. Hans fascination af gladiatorkampe viser vanens magt. Han er til stede under omvendelsen i bog VIII og bliver senere døbt sammen med Augustin.

cast.name: Det ukendte barn
cast.description: Augustin hører et barn synge »Tag og læs« fra et nabohus. Han siger udtrykkeligt, at han ikke ved, om det er en dreng eller en pige. Han opfatter ordene som en guddommelig anvisning og læser et afsnit hos Paulus.

cast.name: Gud
cast.description: Augustin henvender sig til Gud som den, der allerede kender hans liv. Han omtaler også sine menneskelige læsere og taler undertiden direkte til dem. Læseren møder derfor både en bøn og en beretning skrevet for at blive delt.

whyItMatters.title: Selvransagelse gennem fortælling
whyItMatters.body: Hverdagsminder bærer store spørgsmål: Hvorfor stjæle noget, man ikke behøver? Hvorfor nyde sorgen i teatret? Hvorfor søge ros? Og hvorfor kæmpe for at handle efter en fast overbevisning? Man kan diskutere Augustins svar, men bevægelsen mellem en episode og undersøgelsen af dens motiver giver bogen meget af dens styrke.

whyItMatters.title: Omvendelse uden en enkel afslutning
whyItMatters.body: Scenen i haven i bog VIII afslutter ikke undersøgelsen af selvet. Bog X vender tilbage til fristelser knyttet til begær, mad, musik, nysgerrighed og ros. Læs afsnittene sammen, så omvendelsen ikke blot bliver en pæn slutning på historien.

whyItMatters.title: Et argument om tid
whyItMatters.body: Bog XI spørger, hvordan fortid, nutid og fremtid kan forstås, når fortiden er borte, fremtiden endnu ikke er kommet, og nutiden ingen varighed har. Eksempler med tale, stavelser og en velkendt sang fører Augustin frem mod hukommelse, opmærksomhed og forventning. Følg argumentets trin i stedet for kun at læse det berømte spørgsmål som et løsrevet citat.
